commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-one studies tested explanation fidelity, stability, or clinical meaningfulness, and 14 reported favorable results, but 20 were offline or simulated and none compared decisions or patient outcomes with and without pre-release validation. Hazard studies show that explanations are often unfaithful or unstable, which suggests such testing may detect problems, though whether it prevents clinicians from being misled remains untested.

perspectives.view: Twenty of the 21 studies were level 4 or 5 and offline or simulated. The single level 3 study, the only real deployment, rated explanations on 17 patients. No study compared decisions or outcomes with and without pre-release validation. Results varied, with 14 supportive, 6 mixed, and 1 against. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and risk of bias.

In one study, SHAP explanations had 100% fidelity, yet clinicians complied with the AI in 86% of cases. This suggests faithful explanations can still foster over-trust. When AI outputs were wrong, explanations lowered trust in experienced clinicians but did so inconsistently in less experienced ones. In a hazard benchmark, 83.0% of correct chest X-ray predictions had saliency IoU below 0.1.

Expert clinicians agreed with model explanations in 74.2% of cases, and a clinician panel rated them useful in 75.0%. Another study rated 92.6% of explanations useful and linked review to changed management intent in 27.6%. A hazard survey found that physicians' preference for lesion-aligned maps may be superficial, so rater approval may not measure understanding.

FDA draft guidance states that sponsors should validate explainability metrics and visualizations for the target user group. FUTURE-AI asks evaluations to identify limitations such as sensitivity to noise. Stability appears measurable, since explanation divergence rose from 0.144 to 0.251 as sensor noise reached 20%. No study tested whether such requirements change clinical use.

Several user tests relied on panels of 6 to 28 clinicians. No study reported cost, staff time, or repeat testing after model updates. Automated fidelity and stability metrics were computed offline on existing datasets, which may require fewer resources. None of these studies measured how those metrics relate to clinician behavior.

In a vignette study of 776 participants, lay users showed more automation bias with LLM explanations than experienced primary care physicians did. This suggests that explanations shown to patients may raise trust in wrong outputs. No study tested explanations with patients as the target users.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployed tools whose explanations were validated before release with tools that were not. Such comparisons should measure clinician over-reliance, detection of AI errors, and patient outcomes. They should include less experienced clinicians, patient-facing explanations, and repeat validation after model updates or data drift.
commentary.underserved_note: One of the 21 tests, a fidelity analysis of logged decisions, drew on a Medicaid population. No test included safety-net settings, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users, and many did not report their setting. The findings on clinical meaningfulness therefore reflect clinicians in largely unspecified settings and may not apply to these populations.
